## {#jessica-divider}

[Jessica Jack<span class="gold">Getting started, and visualization as a research method</span>]{.divider-name}

```{=html}
<div class="jj-agenda">
  <div><b>1</b><span>Starting point: no coding experience</span></div>
  <div><b>2</b><span>Method: build a visualization, look, change it, repeat</span></div>
  <div><b>3</b><span>Results: what the visualizations showed</span></div>
  <div><b>4</b><span>Checking: failures, and testing what I saw</span></div>
</div>
```

::: notes
0. I'm a PhD student in History at USask, supervised by Jim. My research asks how Saskatchewan's network of settlements turned Indigenous land into private property between 1880 and 1930. This section is about how I got started, and how making visualizations became my research method. Read the four parts out loud. The same four labels sit at the top of every slide in this section.
:::

## Where I started: three datasets, no coding {#jessica-start}

```{=html}
<div class="jj-map"><span class="on">1 Starting point</span><span>2 Method</span><span>3 Results</span><span>4 Checking</span></div>
```

My question: how did Saskatchewan's settlements relate to First Nations losing their land, 1880–1921? That needed **three datasets that had never been joined**:

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .accent}
[Compiled by hand, summer 2025]{.kicker}

#### A knowledge graph

409 of the 429 urban municipalities in the 1921 census, built from more than 200 community-written local histories.
:::

::: {.card}
[GEORIA project, U of Toronto]{.kicker}

#### Railway GIS

Historical Canadian Railroads: every line, with its company and construction date.
:::

::: {.card}
[Mapping Settler Colonialism]{.kicker}

#### Reserve surrenders

54 surrendered parcels on 42 reserves, compiled by Ashley Rabbitskin and Julian Rioux.
:::
:::

[Before 9 January 2026, I had never written code.]{.gold style="font-family: Georgia, serif; font-size: 1.05em;"}

::: notes
0–1. My background is anthropology: a BA, then an MA in medical anthropology. I came to history through mapping on the Sakitawak Traditional Land Use Study in 2024, where Ben Hoy taught me historical GIS software.

I spent summer 2025 in archives and local history collections documenting when and how each settlement was established. I didn't realize at the time that the spreadsheet I was building was a knowledge graph. Jacob will come back to that.

The three datasets were in different formats, at different scales, and built for different purposes. The interesting questions needed all three together. Getting them to talk to each other needed data engineering skills I didn't have.

Sources: working paper (Jack 2026, *Working Papers in Critical Search* 003, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20706174), "The Constraints" and "Code and Data Availability." Before January 9 I had not coded, apart from some basic HTML.
:::

## Skills flattening: what one person can now build {#jessica-flattening}

```{=html}
<div class="jj-map"><span class="on">1 Starting point</span><span>2 Method</span><span>3 Results</span><span>4 Checking</span></div>
```

::: {.def}
[Skills flattening]{.def-term}
The gap between knowing a computer *could* do a task and being able to make it do it has narrowed. I could work in plain English with a coding agent, so I was no longer waiting on someone else's time or skills.
:::

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[$30 CAD]{.num}
[a month: a Claude Pro subscription]{.lbl}
:::

::: {.stat}
[1 laptop]{.num}
[an ordinary consumer laptop; no high-performance computing]{.lbl}
:::

::: {.stat}
[Mid-tier]{.num}
[Claude Sonnet, not the largest model]{.lbl}
:::
:::

What I built from that starting point:

::: {.chips .jj-chips}
[a Neo4j knowledge graph]{.hit} [25 interactive visualizations]{.hit} [two public websites]{.c} [entity extraction from 142 local histories]{.c} [6,061 people linked across court records]{.c}
:::

::: notes
2–3. This is the core of "skills flattening." Each of these used to need a programmer, a web developer or a data team.

Sources: the working paper's "Computational Resources" section (Pro subscription, $20 USD / $30 CAD a month; Claude Sonnet, claude-sonnet-4-5 then claude-sonnet-4-6; a consumer laptop, no HPC). Counts: 25 HTML visualizations in `Sask_Railway_Visualizations`; the public sites are Sask_Railway_Visualizations and Sask_Community_Sources on jjax07.github.io; 142 books in `OCR_NER/README.md`; 6,061 people in `Summer_JP_Work/README.md` (`Stable_ID_Roster_v6.csv`).

The mid-tier model mattered: Sonnet is more prone to easy but incorrect solutions, so I had to check outputs closely. Usage limits made me plan each session deliberately. That rigour became part of the method.
:::

## Before: each new version of a map took days {#jessica-old}

```{=html}
<div class="jj-map"><span>1 Starting point</span><span class="on">2 Method</span><span>3 Results</span><span>4 Checking</span></div>
```

> GIS software could map the data, but this software limited the kinds of questions I could ask.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Constraint 1]{.kicker}

#### Translation

Three datasets in different formats, scales and purposes. Joining them needed a data engineer, or a lot of my time.
:::

::: {.card}
[Constraint 2]{.kicker}

#### Scale

429 municipalities, half a province, 50 years, on an MA timeline. Case studies were possible; the bigger picture was not.
:::

::: {.card}
[Constraint 3]{.kicker}

#### Code

Learning to program mid-degree would have pulled my energy away from the historical problem and toward the technical one.
:::
:::

::: notes
3–4. With desktop GIS such as ArcGIS, the software dictated the output. Each version of a map took days, so you made few versions and rarely tried an idea you weren't already sure of. The alternatives were pre-built tools designed for other purposes, or not asking the question at all.

Quote and the three constraints: working paper, "The Constraints."
:::

## Now: each new version takes minutes {#jessica-loop .motion}

```{=html}
<div class="jj-map"><span>1 Starting point</span><span class="on">2 Method</span><span>3 Results</span><span>4 Checking</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node rise" data-at="300"><b>Describe</b><span>a research question, in plain English</span></div>
  <div class="arrow" data-at="900">→</div>
  <div class="node blue rise" data-at="1200"><b>Generate</b><span>a visualization from the data</span></div>
  <div class="arrow" data-at="1800">→</div>
  <div class="node rise" data-at="2100"><b>React</b><span>what works, what's missing, what's unexpected</span></div>
  <div class="arrow" data-at="2700">→</div>
  <div class="node rise" data-at="3000"><b>Next prompt</b><span>the reaction drives the next question</span></div>
</div>
<div class="loopback" data-at="3800">↺ again, and again: within one session, not across weeks</div>
<p class="motion-caption rise" data-at="4800" style="font-size:1.1em;font-family:Georgia,serif;">Each new version: <span class="jj-days">days</span> <span class="mk" data-at="5600">minutes</span></p>
<blockquote class="rise" data-at="6600">Being able to test an idea within a session rather than across weeks changed which ideas were worth testing.</blockquote>
```

::: notes
4–5. Animated, about 7 seconds. This cycle is the basic unit of the work. A question that might have been set aside as too ambitious or too uncertain became worth pursuing when the cost of trying it was an afternoon rather than a month.

Loop wording and quote: working paper, abstract and "The Process."
:::

> I have lived in Saskatchewan my whole life and have experienced its distances, but seeing them in railway time rather than driving time shifted my thinking.

The myth of the lone pioneer started to give way.

[These places were not isolated. They were nodes in a network, and the network had a shape.]{.gold}

5–6. The clip plays by itself: Saskatoon's one-hour reach by train, 1890 to 1920. Built within days of my first session, and the first thing I pushed to GitHub to share with Jim and colleagues.

One hour means 40 km at 40 km/h, a proxy for branch-line speeds, which varied.

[TBD: check before the talk. In the clip's sidebar, Osler shows "132.8 km by rail" and Dalmeny "127.5 km by rail," yet both count as within one hour. The Settlement Explorer filters by actual rail distance; this map may not.]

Quote: working paper, "The Process." Clip recorded from the local `Sask_Railway_Visualizations` repository by `scripts/record_jessica_clips.py`.

```{=html}
<div class="jj-map"><span>1 Starting point</span><span>2 Method</span><span class="on">3 Results</span><span>4 Checking</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
```{=html}
<video class="jj-clip" data-autoplay muted playsinline controls poster="images/jessica/economic-hierarchy-poster.jpg">
  <source src="images/jessica/economic-hierarchy.mp4" type="video/mp4">

</video>
```

[Economic Hierarchy, Saskatchewan 1921: tiers switched on from cities down to elevator sidings. [Open it live](https://jjax07.github.io/Sask_Railway_Visualizations/economic_hierarchy.html)]{.caption}
:::

::: {.column width="36%"}
::: {.jj-side}
Were these "urban municipalities" really urban, or just farms with a post office? The census occupations answered it.

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[79%]{.num}
[of working residents in **farm villages** held non-farming jobs: 17,138 of 21,708 with a classifiable occupation, 1921 census]{.lbl}
:::
:::

Grain buyers, bank clerks, blacksmiths, station agents. The typology became a central framework of my thesis.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
9–10. The clip turns on each tier in turn: 7 cities, 39 regional hubs, 27 service towns and 356 farm villages from the 1921 census. Then come 435 grain hamlets and 69 elevator sidings from grain elevator licensing records (1911–1930). Tiers cluster in unexpected places, which pointed to forces beyond local settler demand.

79%: 17,138 of 21,708 farm-village residents with a classifiable occupation (`KnowledgeGraph/analysis/NAMED_ROLES_SYNTHESIS.md`). "Agricultural" means a farming occupation title or a farming industry ("Own Farm," "Agriculture"). If someone asks about the "nine in ten" from the CHA talk: by job title alone it's nine in ten; counting farm labourers by the industry they worked in, it's four in five. Same as the Active History post, 14 October 2026.
:::

## A pattern in a map needs a statistical test {#jessica-question}

```{=html}
<div class="jj-map"><span>1 Starting point</span><span>2 Method</span><span>3 Results</span><span class="on">4 Checking</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{=html}
<img class="jj-img" src="images/jessica/reserve-surrender-overlay.jpg" alt="Map of settlements coloured by when they were founded relative to the nearest reserve surrender, with surrendered reserve land and railway lines">
```
[Settlements by timing relative to the nearest reserve surrender, with surrendered land and railway lines.]{.caption}
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.jj-side}
::: {.def}
[Reserve surrender]{.def-term}
A legal process under the Indian Act by which a First Nation gave up part of its reserve land to the Crown, usually for sale to settlers, often under heavy pressure.
:::

Surrendered land clustered near railway lines. That was **a question to test**, not yet a finding.

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[+77%]{.num}
[odds of surrender per extra 1,000 rural settlers within 25 km. Logistic regression, 128 reserves: OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.44–2.17, p < 0.001]{.lbl}
:::
:::

> The skepticism and professional rigour that AI requires are not a caveat. They are the method.
:::
:::

The test: logistic regression on all 128 reserves, surrendered ~ rural population within 25 km (per 1,000). Odds ratio 1.77, 95% CI 1.44–2.17, p < 0.001, AUC 0.835 (`Reserves_Urban_Spaces/analysis/06b_LOGISTIC_REGRESSION_SYNTHESIS.md`, model M1). Say "odds," not "probability."
